title: Is it ever OK to lie?
summary: Steelman the other side, back up your points with claim, reason, example, then debate whether it is ever OK to lie.

steps.title: Philosophy meets debate
steps.body:
This week the debate topic is also a real philosophy question, not just a fun one: is it ever OK to lie? Philosophers have argued about this for centuries, and there is no single right answer, which is exactly what makes it worth debating properly.

Steelman first, same rule as before: before you argue your own side, say the other side's best point, in your own words, the strongest version of it, not a weak one. If you are arguing that lying can be OK, first say the strongest reason someone might think lying is always wrong. If you are arguing that lying is always wrong, first say the strongest reason someone might think a lie can be OK.

Back up every point with claim, reason, example: state your claim plainly, give one reason it is true, then back it with a real or made-up example a listener can picture. 'Lying is sometimes OK' is a claim on its own, it only becomes convincing once you add why and show it with an example.

Two examples to think about before the debate. A lie that protects someone: telling a friend hiding from danger that you have not seen them, when you have. A lie that helps yourself: telling a teacher you finished your homework when you did not. Are these the same kind of lie? Three rounds of debate, and the motion is the question itself: it is sometimes OK to lie.

steps.title: Record it
steps.prompt: Record part of the debate, or record yourself afterward explaining the difference between a lie that protects someone and a lie that helps yourself.
